title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
title_bn: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
paragraph1: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark? Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye.
paragraph2: A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn early to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team going out on the field together. And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other.
paragraph3: That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer. Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark? Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor.  .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn. I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda. Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.] Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday. Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light.
paragraph4: We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking. Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal. You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal? Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it. Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else did. It’s never happened? Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset. Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities .
paragraph5: . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner. Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace? Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff. One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory? Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us.
bangla_paragraph1: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark? Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye.
bangla_paragraph2: A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn early to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team going out on the field together. And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other.
bangla_paragraph3: That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer. Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark? Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor.  .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn. I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda. Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.] Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday. Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light.
bangla_paragraph4: We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking. paragraph1: Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good. Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value.
paragraph2: And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study.
paragraph3: But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.

title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
title_bn: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
author: TechPulse
excerpt: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
paragraph1: “You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film. The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic.
paragraph2: The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries. But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing. While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.) TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday.
paragraph3: She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey. The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend, and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10.
paragraph4: And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
title_bn: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The outside watchdog can publish its findings without Anthropic's approval.
paragraph1: “If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance,” the company said. Anthropic is also under pressure to reassure investors that safety issues will not overshadow its initial public offering, expected this year at a more than $2tn valuation. It devoted a large part of investor presentations this week to laying out its safety practices. METR was one of the organisations that investigated the hack of Hugging Face by rogue OpenAI models, reviewing thousands of logs and receiving company laptops.
paragraph2: Anthropic has now onboarded six METR employees, giving them company hardware, office space and “access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to.” The lab said it has encouraged employees to share information with the evaluators as they would with a fellow employee working in risk. Anthropic is not paying METR for this arrangement. The research group does not accept donations from AI companies or their staff.
paragraph3: It is funded by donations from individuals and philanthropic organisations, as well as government bodies such as the UK’s AI Security Institute. The evaluators will publish their analysis, and Anthropic cannot veto publication. However, it can require them to redact information that falls into certain categories, such as customer data, details covered by attorney-client privilege or information about model architectures. Anthropic added it was still working with Accenture, which was named a partner on safety testing last month, with each committing at least $1 billion to set up new safeguards.
paragraph4: Another third-party tester is SecureBio, which reviews chemical and biological weapon risk for the company. “We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same,” Anthropic said. METR was one of the organisations that investigated the hack of Hugging Face by rogue OpenAI models, reviewing thousands of logs and receiving company laptops.
bangla_paragraph2: Anthropic has now onboarded six METR employees, giving them company hardware, office space and “access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to.” The lab said it has encouraged employees to share information with the evaluators as they would with a fellow employee working in risk. Anthropic is not paying METR for this arrangement. The research group does not accept donations from AI companies or their staff.
bangla_paragraph3: It is funded by donations from individuals and philanthropic organisations, as well as government bodies such as the UK’s AI Security Institute. The evaluators will publish their analysis, and Anthropic cannot veto publication. However, it can require them to redact information that falls into certain categories, such as customer data, details covered by attorney-client privilege or information about model architectures. Anthropic added it was still working with Accenture, which was named a partner on safety testing last month, with each committing at least $1 billion to set up new safeguards.
bangla_paragraph4: Another third-party tester is SecureBio, which reviews chemical and biological weapon risk for the company. “We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same,” Anthropic said. METR said: “We stand ready to work with all frontier AI developers to bring better evidence to the public.” © 2026 The Financial Times Ltd.

title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
title_bn: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
paragraph1: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility! As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe, I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either. Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon, a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software. Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer.
paragraph2: (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.) Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.” So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.” Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals. And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles. “Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities.
paragraph3: It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.” Deals! Image Credits:Bryce Durbin Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million, Axios reported, citing sources. Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing. Evos, a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures. Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures. PlusAI, the autonomous trucking developer, and Texas Ventures Acquisition III filed a Form S-4 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission —advancing its previously announced agreement to go public via a merger with a blank-check company. Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. Neither company shared financial terms of the deal. The automaker plans to use a trio of Nvidia products to be able to offer hands-free, point-to-point driving on highways and surface streets. Waabi, a startup developing self-driving trucks, landed a commercial partnership with carrier Warrior Logistics.
paragraph4: Under the deal, Waabi’s self-driving trucks will move freight between Dallas and Houston. Notable reads and other tidbits Image Credits:Bryce Durbin Electric vehicle sales in the United States are showing signs of life. Laplace Intelligence, one of 20 startups that competed in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200, is building automated red-teaming that stress-tests robots and self-driving cars. MIT startup LNK Energies says it has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from price spikes. The Paris Auto Show puts Chinese cars on center stage. Tesla showcased its SpaceX-powered Roadster with a theatrical kickflip stunt. The Roadster used a mix of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and stick a landing on the pavement below. CEO Elon Musk claims the vehicle will be on the road by 2028. But will future owners be allowed to legally deploy these maneuvers on public streets? I don’t see how. Waymo is expanding into Canada — specifically, Toronto — after receiving approval to participate in an automated vehicle pilot program. Waymo has also opened up its robotaxi service to everyone, meaning no more waitlists, in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa. One more thing … The electric Macan’s roofline is slightly more bulbous than the gas-burning version.

title: Mark Gurman: Apple Made 'Major Mistake' With iPhone Duo Pre-Orders
title_bn: Mark Gurman: Apple Made 'Major Mistake' With iPhone Duo Pre-Orders
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Despite knowing that the iPhone Duo would face "severe supply constraints" due to manufacturing challenges, Apple chose to begin iPhone Duo pre-orders on Friday instead of waiting until it had more inventory ready, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurma
paragraph1: Despite knowing that the iPhone Duo would face "severe supply constraints" due to manufacturing challenges, Apple chose to begin iPhone Duo pre-orders on Friday instead of waiting until it had more inventory ready, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. In his Power On newsletter today, he called this decision a "major mistake." "Let me cut to the chase: Apple made a major mistake here," he said. "The company knew there would be severe supply constraints but went ahead with the launch anyway, apparently prioritizing a desire to get the device on the market early in its fiscal first quarter over satisfying demand. That will disappoint many of the early adopters most eager to buy it."
paragraph2: Apple originally planned to launch the iPhone Duo in the U.S. and China only before expanding the device to other countries later, according to Gurman, but the company ultimately decided to start pre-orders in more than 70 countries simultaneously. Less than 30 minutes after pre-orders began, Apple's estimated shipping dates for the iPhone Duo slipped to around January 25 in most countries. Apple typically underpromises and overdelivers with its delivery dates, though, so hopefully some customers will end up having their shipping estimates bumped up at least slightly.

title: Asus ROG Strix XG27AQGNV 27-inch G-Sync Pulsar gaming monitor review: Super smooth with unprecedented control
title_bn: Asus ROG Strix XG27AQGNV 27-inch G-Sync Pulsar gaming monitor review: Super smooth with unprecedented control
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Asus delivers its take on G-Sync Pulsar with the ROG Strix XG27AQGNV. This 27-inch IPS panel sports smooth motion with 360 Hz, QHD resolution, HDR and wide gamut color.
paragraph1: G-Sync Pulsar delivers OLED-level smoothness, responsiveness, and gaming feel to LCD monitors, and the Asus ROG Strix XG27AQNGV is a great example. With unmatched tweakability, it will satisfy gamers from casual to professional. Reasons to buy +G-Sync Pulsar delivers OLED-level smoothness and responsiveness +Fine and precise control of gamma and luminance +400-step variable overdrive +Accurate color +Premium build quality Reasons to avoid -Smaller color gamut than other speedy monitors -No dynamic dimming means HDR contrast is the same as SDR Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Go to page: In the evolution of gaming monitors, there is nothing more significant than the advent of G-Sync and FreeSync (AKA, Adaptive-Sync or VRR). By syncing the video card output and monitor refresh rate in real time, all frame tearing and stuttering are eliminated.
paragraph2: But there is one thing this tech cannot fix – motion blur.LCD panels continuously display each frame until the next one arrives. This inevitably results in blur unless frame rates are very high. At least 500Hz is needed to truly call LCD motion resolution perfect. How to combat this? Well, you can buy one of the best OLED gaming monitors, which has a much faster panel response.

title: Only 8% of fund managers report improved investment returns from AI adoption: Morgan Stanley–Oliver Wyman
title_bn: Only 8% of fund managers report improved investment returns from AI adoption: Morgan Stanley–Oliver Wyman
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Despite growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global asset management industry, only 8 per cent of fund managers have reported measurable improvements in investment returns, according to a joint research report by Morgan Stanley and
paragraph1: Despite growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global asset management industry, only 8 per cent of fund managers have reported measurable improvements in investment returns, according to a joint research report by Morgan Stanley and Oliver Wyman.Only 8% of fund managers report improved investment returns from AI adoption: Morgan Stanley–Oliver WymanNew Delhi [India], October 18 (ANI): Despite growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global asset management industry, only 8 per cent of fund managers have reported measurable improvements in investment returns, according to a joint research report by Morgan Stanley and Oliver Wyman.The findings highlight a gap between the increasing use of AI by investment firms and its ability to deliver better returns for investors.
paragraph2: The September 2026 BluePaper report, titled Breaking from the Pack: The Race for Above-Market Growth, cited the Mercer 2026 AI in Asset Management Survey, which found that 55 per cent of asset managers had integrated AI into at least one part of their investment process, while another 27 per cent were testing applications.However, the benefits have largely remained limited to operational efficiency and research capabilities."Notably, investment returns have not yet seen widespread impacts from AI, with just 8% of firms reporting measurable benefits," the report stated.
paragraph3: According to the survey, 69 per cent of asset managers reported improved operational efficiency, while 55 per cent cited better insights and decision-making. However, only 24 per cent reported reduced costs.AI adoption was strongest in investment research, where 49 per cent of firms had integrated the technology, followed by data processing at 40 per cent.
paragraph4: Its use remained limited in core investment decisions, with only 13 per cent integrating AI into portfolio construction and 7 per cent into trade execution."Whether greater research breadth ultimately translates into persistent alpha remains unproven," the report said, referring to returns above market benchmarks.The report also cautioned that faster research and improved productivity do not necessarily translate into financial gains."
paragraph5: However, productivity gains do not automatically translate into enterprise-wide financial impact," it stated.The findings suggest that while AI is helping investment firms process information faster, its ability to consistently improve investor returns remains uncertain.

title: MIT engineers build soft 3D shape-sensing skin for gaming and VR
title_bn: MIT engineers build soft 3D shape-sensing skin for gaming and VR
author: TechPulse
excerpt: MIT engineers embedded soft optical fibers in a silicone sheet that reconstructs its own 3D shape, aimed at gaming, VR, and physical therapy.
paragraph1: (Image credit: MIT, courtesy of the researchers; edited by MIT News) MIT engineers have built a soft, wearable shape-sensing sheet with self-tracking movement that could be useful for controlling games, virtual reality, and physical therapy applications, reports MIT News. The technology, which leverages optical fibers to track the sheet’s own 3D shape, keeps its error below half a centimeter in lab tests.
paragraph2: Qifan Yu, an MIT mechanical engineering graduate student on the team, put rigid-sensor designs at around 1 to 2 cm and called the result “at least on par with existing technologies.” The sheet also still works even when damaged, but the fibers remain thicker than ideal for garments.
paragraph3: The news follows a paper, “Toward fully soft and multifunctional shape sensing via optical waveguide arrays,” recently published in Advanced Intelligent Systems. It details that the waveguides respond to bending in both directions, “bi-directional,” with the array laid out to discern shapes.
paragraph4: Combined fiber responses mean fewer sensing elements are needed, and that can also improve damage resilience. The fibers respond to pressure, so they can sense external force, such as a press on the forearm in a physical therapy demo.

title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
title_bn: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
author: TechPulse
excerpt: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for
paragraph1: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.How it startedThe first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
paragraph2: While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.How it’s goingMunicipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle.
paragraph3: They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
paragraph4: What happens nextAs the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
paragraph5: By the wayEven if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.Read thisStreetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports.Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

title: MeitY-backed conclave explores AI applications in healthcare, assistive technologies
title_bn: MeitY-backed conclave explores AI applications in healthcare, assistive technologies
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Artificial intelligence could improve disease screening, medical diagnostics and remote patient monitoring while making healthcare more accessible and affordable, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) S. Krishnan
paragraph1: Artificial intelligence could improve disease screening, medical diagnostics and remote patient monitoring while making healthcare more accessible and affordable, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) S. Krishnan said at a technology conclave in Varanasi, highlighting the potential of AI-driven solutions to address healthcare and accessibility needs.MeitY-backed conclave explores AI applications in healthcare, assistive technologiesNew Delhi [India], October 18 (ANI): Artificial intelligence could improve disease screening, medical diagnostics and remote patient monitoring while making healthcare more accessible and affordable, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) S. Krishnan said at a technology conclave in Varanasi, highlighting the potential of AI-driven solutions to address healthcare and accessibility needs.
paragraph2: The conclave on “AI for Health & Assistive Technologies” was organised by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI), under MeitY, and the Centre for Innovation, Incubation and Entrepreneurship (CIIE) at IIT BHU, bringing together government representatives, healthcare professionals, researchers and startups to explore practical applications of artificial intelligence.Delivering the keynote address, Krishnan emphasised the role of AI in strengthening clinical decision-making and improving healthcare service delivery, particularly for communities with limited access to medical facilities.He highlighted potential applications ranging from disease screening and medical diagnostics to remote intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring and AI-assisted surgical planning. He also stressed the need to integrate AI education across disciplines and strengthen collaboration between technology institutions, medical sciences, researchers and startups to develop scalable solutions.
paragraph3: Krishnan further highlighted support available through the IndiaAI Mission and other MeitY initiatives to encourage innovation in the sector.STPI Director General Arvind Kumar called for building on India's experience in developing its information technology and IT-enabled services industry to promote indigenous AI innovation and entrepreneurship.Highlighting STPI's network of 27 Centres of Entrepreneurship, Kumar underlined the importance of translational research, intellectual property creation and market access in helping startups take innovative ideas to commercial applications. He also emphasised the need to strengthen startup ecosystems beyond established technology hubs through collaboration between academic institutions, industry and government.
paragraph4: The conclave featured panel discussions on empowering citizens through AI in healthcare, inclusion and well-being, and translating AI research into scalable healthcare and assistive technology solutions.The discussions brought together experts from academia, healthcare institutions, government and startups to examine how research and technological innovation could be converted into practical solutions addressing societal needs.IIT BHU Director Amit Patra highlighted the institution's efforts to strengthen its startup ecosystem through CIIE, with a focus on nurturing entrepreneurial thinking among students and faculty, connecting innovators with funding sources and building a sustainable pipeline of startups.The programme underscored the importance of collaboration between government, academia, healthcare institutions and startups in developing accessible, responsible and scalable AI solutions.

title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
title_bn: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
paragraph1: U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices. They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices.Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product.Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve.“There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney.Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper.“We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote.But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation.
paragraph2: For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said.Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law.Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny.What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing.Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S.
paragraph3: changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager.What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags.Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology.The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced.“Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said.What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing" for the same practice.Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices.
paragraph4: An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers.Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut’s legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases.California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer's app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside.Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using so-called geofencing technology to increase prices.Target said the app functionality at issue was used to “provide guests with accurate pricing, which can vary across stores and channels.” The retailer said it didn't personalize prices based on a guest’s data or behavior and remains “committed to clear, transparent pricing.”Different prices do not necessarily mean personal data was used. Last year, an investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that shoppers on Instacart were shown different prices for identical products at the same stores. Instacart subsequently ended what it described as tests that randomly assigned shoppers to groups rather than setting prices based on their personal information.What it is: Algorithmic pricing uses software to recommend or automatically set prices. Companies have used such systems for decades. AI can help the software identify patterns in sales, competitors’ prices and other information to predict demand and estimate how different prices would affect sales and profits.
paragraph5: These tools can support both dynamic and personalized pricing.Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely retailers use AI to help set prices, but research suggests businesses across industries are adopting it.Simon-Kucher, a global consulting company, surveyed more than 2,200 business leaders in 28 countries and 39 industries last year, and 41% said they used AI software to gather market intelligence, including competitors’ prices. Another 28% said they used it for “real-time price optimization.” Price optimization means choosing prices that advance business goals, such as increasing profits, attracting shoppers or clearing unsold goods.The National Retail Federation, which represents big and small stores, said algorithmic pricing is a new method of doing what retailers have always done: monitor and adjust prices depending on supply, demand, seasonality, competitors' prices and other factors.Some lawsuits have alleged companies used pricing algorithms to undermine competition.A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged, among other practices, an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie. The agency alleged Amazon used the tool to identify products whose prices it could raise with competitors likely to follow, generating more than $1 billion in excess profits.A trial is scheduled for next year. Amazon said the FTC allegations “grossly mischaracterize” the pricing tool.Project Nessie was intended to stop retail price-matching practices from creating unsustainably low prices, the e-commerce giant said.

title: Apple October 2026 launches: Touchscreen MacBook Pro, M6 iMac, OLED iPad Mini and more expected
title_bn: Apple October 2026 launches: Touchscreen MacBook Pro, M6 iMac, OLED iPad Mini and more expected
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Apple could announce a touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6-powered iMac and an OLED iPad mini by the end of October 2026. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has invited select media members to a product event in Los Angeles on October 28.
paragraph1: Apple could announce a touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6-powered iMac and an OLED iPad mini by the end of October 2026. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has invited select media members to a product event in Los Angeles on October 28.Apple October 2026 Event.(MattTalkTech)Apple could announce several new products in the final days of October 2026, including a touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6-powered iMac and an OLED iPad mini. Apple has invited a group of media persons to a product event on 28 October in Los Angeles, according to Mark Gurman of Bloomberg. The company isn't planning on holding a traditional livestream but rather a hands-on demonstration.The expected launches can bring a lot of changes in Apple's Mac and iPad lineup, including the addition of touchscreen technology to the MacBook Pro lineup. However, Apple has yet to officially declare most of these products or their release dates. The iPhone Duo’s October availability and a high-memory Mac Studio configuration are among the hardware announcements the company has confirmed.
paragraph2: Apple October event: What to expectAccording to Gurman’s report for Bloomberg, Apple may start announcing new products around October 27, earlier than the media event on October 28. Additionally, MacRumors has covered a few hardware releases and software upgrades that might be released this month.Here is what could arrive before the end of October.OLED touchscreen MacBook ProThe most significant among the potential announcements is a new, redesigned MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen. Apple may also release a thinner and lighter version of the 14-inch and 16-inch models, according to a report by MacRumors.The OLED panel could take the place of the current mini-LED panel, with better contrast and deeper blacks. Touch input is expected to be an enhancement of the keyboard and trackpad. The new models, though, might be powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, rather than the new M6 Pro and M6 Max processors. Apple has yet to confirm the rollout schedule.
paragraph3: M6 MacBook Pro and iMacAnother possibility is that Apple could release a 14-inch MacBook Pro with its expected M6 chipset. Another option is to get a new 24-inch iMac with the same chip, new colours and performance enhancements for the desktop.These products remain unconfirmed, and reports differ on whether the M6-powered models will arrive alongside the redesigned OLED MacBook Pro.OLED iPad mini and software updatesApple is also known to be working on an OLED iPad Mini. The existing reports suggest the tablet will be powered by the A20 Pro chipset, will have a front camera with landscape orientation, modified speakers and better water resistance. The company hasn't declared any specifications or release date.It may also be software features that are scheduled for Apple in October. iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.
paragraph4: 2 and macOS 27.2 could be coming sometime this month, which could mean more Siri AI language support. Apple has not announced a release date.What Apple has officially confirmedThe iPhone Duo will be available in India from October 23, and pre-orders will open at 5:30 PM on October 16, Apple has announced. The company has also announced that it will have a unified memory configuration of 512GB available in the Mac Studio by the end of October.The touchscreen MacBook Pro, M6 MacBook Pro, OLED iPad mini and M6 iMac are all reported launches at this time. Apple’s final announcements and availability dates could differ from current expectations.About the AuthorPragya Singha RoyPragya is a Technology reporter with over four years of experience in digital media and content writing. She holds a Master’s degree in Journalism and has covered a wide range of stories spanning space, smartphones, gadgets, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and the ways technology is transforming everyday life.
paragraph5: She focuses on breaking down complex technology and science developments into clear, engaging, and reader-friendly stories, with a keen interest in emerging trends and their real-world impact. Before joining her current newsroom, Pragya worked with News9Live, where she covered the technology beat extensively, reporting on smartphones, consumer technology, AI, space and science, while also contributing to video and visual content. Her experience includes breaking news, explainers, SEO-driven stories, product coverage, interviews, unboxing videos and live event reporting. She has also covered major technology and AI events, giving her experience in both newsroom and on-ground reporting. Beyond journalism, Pragya is an avid gamer and a passionate reader of fiction. She enjoys exploring immersive worlds through games and books, with a particular interest in stories that offer new perspectives, ideas, and experiences.

title: Indian Startup IPO Tracker 2026
title_bn: Indian Startup IPO Tracker 2026
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping…
paragraph1: Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “⁠Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fifteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses.
paragraph2: Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty seven startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs.

title: Burma Burma Parent’s FY26 Loss Surges 31X YoY To ₹15 Cr
title_bn: Burma Burma Parent’s FY26 Loss Surges 31X YoY To ₹15 Cr
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Restaurant chain Burma Burma’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, saw its net loss skyrocket nearly 31X to ₹15.4 Cr in…
paragraph1: SUMMARYThe restaurant chain’s revenue from operations also zoomed 46.6% to ₹155.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹106.1 Cr in FY25 This comes as Burma Burma has filed its DRHP with the SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue worth up to ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.8 Cr shares On the operational front, the restaurant chain’s EBITDA also climbed 20.2% to ₹25.7 Cr in FY26. Meanwhile, total expenses rose 61.8% YoY to ₹175.8 Cr Restaurant chain Burma Burma’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, saw its net loss skyrocket nearly 31X to ₹15.4 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26) compared to ₹50 Lakh in the previous fiscal year. According to its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP), the restaurant chain’s revenue from operations also zoomed 46.
paragraph2: 6% to ₹155.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹106.1 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹1.5 Cr, Burma Burma’s total income stood at ₹157 Cr in FY26. On the operational front, the restaurant chain’s EBITDA also climbed 20.2% to ₹25.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹21.4 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Besides its FY26 financials, the DRHP also shed light on the company’s Q1 FY27 numbers. Burma Burma’s parent reported a net profit of ₹1.1 Cr in the quarter under review against an operating revenue of ₹53.
paragraph3: 7 Cr. Given total expenses of ₹55.2 Cr during the quarter, what helped the company mint a profit in Q1 FY27 was ₹1.98 Cr in deferred tax credits. Burma Burma also reported an EBITDA profit of ₹11.4 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, while the EBITDA margin stood at 21.3%. Founded in 2013 by Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer, Hunger Pangs operates premium casual restaurant chain Burma Burma, which serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine. It competes with the likes of brands such as Mainland China, Mamagoto, Yum Yum Cha, and Berco’s. At the end of July 2026, it operated 22 restaurants across nine cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata, and Delhi NCR. After raising $4 Mn at a valuation of over $50 Mn earlier this year, the hospitality chain has now filed its DRHP with markets regulator SEBI. Its proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.
paragraph4: 8 Cr shares. Of the fresh IPO proceeds, Burma Burma plans to use ₹117.3 Cr to open 27 new company-owned outlets by FY29. The remaining capital will be used for general corporate purposes. Notably, Hunger Pangs disclosed in its DRHP that it plans to launch a new brand. “We have conceptualised a premium casual dining chain of Japanese restaurants and noodle shops, with influences of Buddhist traditions,” read the document. Where Did Burma Burma Spend In FY26? In line with its revenue growth, Burma Burma’s spending also saw a major uptick. The company’s total expenses zoomed 61.8% YoY to ₹175.8 Cr in FY26. Let’s dive deeper into the company’s expenditure.
paragraph5: Employee Benefits Expenses: Representing the company’s largest cost head, Burma Burma’s personnel costs surged 53.3% YoY to ₹50.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹33.1 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Cost Of Materials Consumed: Burma Burma spent ₹30.4 Cr on raw materials and kitchen supplies in the fiscal under review, 51% higher than ₹20.1 Cr in FY25. Finance Cost: The restaurant chain’s interest and borrowing-related expenses grew 70% YoY to ₹6.6 Cr in the year under review. Other Expenses: Spending under this line item also grew 54.6% YoY to ₹48.8 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
title_bn: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
author: TechPulse
excerpt: A Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
paragraph1: Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services. According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models.
paragraph2: (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.) However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
paragraph3: And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement.
paragraph4: “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.

excerpt: Apple has hired former Meta lawyer Scott Tucker to lead its litigation team, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Tucker will become Apple's vice president of global litigation and financial services, a new position overseeing commercial lawsuits, p
paragraph1: Apple has hired former Meta lawyer Scott Tucker to lead its litigation team, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Tucker will become Apple's vice president of global litigation and financial services, a new position overseeing commercial lawsuits, patent disputes, and legal matters involving its financial products. He previously led litigation at ‌Meta‌ and held a senior legal role at Morgan Stanley. The move brings Tucker back together with Jennifer Newstead, Apple's general counsel. Newstead joined Apple's leadership in March after six years as ‌Meta‌'s top lawyer. Heather Grenier, who currently oversees Apple's commercial and competition litigation, will report to Tucker instead of Newstead.
paragraph2: She will remain on Newstead's leadership team. Apple is also expanding legal executive Kyle Andeer's responsibilities to include international legal matters, child safety, cybersecurity, and law enforcement. The changes are part of a wider overhaul under Newstead, who now oversees both legal and government affairs. Apple announced plans to combine the teams alongside the retirements of Kate Adams and Lisa Jackson. According to Gurman, some Apple executives believe the company should have performed better in court, particularly in App Store disputes. Its battle with Epic Games has forced changes to the rules for links to outside payment options and the fees Apple can charge.
paragraph3: Apple also faces the U.S. government's antitrust lawsuit and privacy cases. Separately, it agreed to a $250 million settlement over delayed Siri features, with a final approval hearing scheduled for February 2027. title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
title_bn: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
paragraph1: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt. Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.
paragraph2: Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.
paragraph3: 5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.
